title: Quantum memories at finite temperature
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/1411.6643v4
published: 2014-11-24T21:08:19Z
summary: To use quantum systems for technological applications we first need to preserve their coherence for macroscopic timescales, even at finite temperature. Quantum error correction has made it possible to actively correct errors that affect a quantum memory. An attractive scenario is the construction of passive storage of quantum information with minimal active support. Indeed, passive protection is the basis of robust and scalable classical technology, physically realized in the form of the transistor and the ferromagnetic hard disk. The discovery of an analogous quantum system is a challenging open problem, plagued with a variety of no-go theorems. Several approaches have been devised to overcome these theorems by taking advantage of their loopholes. Here we review the state-of-the-art developments in this field in an informative and pedagogical way. We give the main principles of self-correcting quantum memories and we analyze several milestone examples from the literature of two-, three- and higher-dimensional quantum memories.

title: Navigating the State of Cognitive Flow: Context-Aware AI Interventions for Effective Reasoning Support
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/2504.16021v1
published: 2025-04-22T16:35:39Z
summary: Flow theory describes an optimal cognitive state where individuals experience deep focus and intrinsic motivation when a task's difficulty aligns with their skill level. In AI-augmented reasoning, interventions that disrupt the state of cognitive flow can hinder rather than enhance decision-making. This paper proposes a context-aware cognitive augmentation framework that adapts interventions based on three key contextual factors: type, timing, and scale. By leveraging multimodal behavioral cues (e.g., gaze behavior, typing hesitation, interaction speed), AI can dynamically adjust cognitive support to maintain or restore flow. We introduce the concept of cognitive flow, an extension of flow theory in AI-augmented reasoning, where interventions are personalized, adaptive, and minimally intrusive. By shifting from static interventions to context-aware augmentation, our approach ensures that AI systems support deep engagement in complex decision-making and reasoning without disrupting cognitive immersion.

Consider an automatic thermostat that adjusts a home heater based on room temperatures. If the thermometer is placed near a hot draft, the thermostat makes flawed decisions for the whole house. Similarly, our computer workers study how software systems examine their own starting rules to prevent logical errors. [1, 2]

Recent paper-supported readings suggest that neuro-symbolic rule-based frameworks can help models conduct error correction in unfamiliar environments. At the same time, automated reasoning models exhibit distinct safety failure profiles under adversarial pressure, which prevents universal self-correction strategies. [1, 2]

Autonomous discovery systems face critical challenges in iterative experiment refinement and independent goal generation. Research teams also note that multi-turn workflows exhibit structural gaps in artificial intelligence identity, lacking persistent memory and verifiable continuity across agent trajectories. [3, 4]

Cultural transmission acts as a domain-general mechanism enabling agents to acquire behavioral dispositions in real-time, while empirical survey data from athletes reveals a serial association model linking training recommendation dependence to reduced autonomy. General preference oracle formulations provide another lens for evaluating agent alignment without relying exclusively on fixed reward functions. [5, 6, 7]

Separating cognition, control, and memory in agent architectures reduces unsupported assertions and improves goal fidelity compared to standard prompt-based baselines. Autonomous systems can also leverage curiosity-driven learning and self-generated goals to explore unstructured problem spaces and accelerate skill acquisition. [8, 9]

Autonomous agentic harnesses can successfully perform scientific algorithm discovery using multi-round search and integrated evaluation. Multi-agent deep reinforcement learning systems employ structured communication across nine architectural dimensions to manage information exchange, while computational creativity frameworks integrate problem formulation with systematic evaluation methods to ensure generated outputs satisfy specific novelty requirements. [10, 11, 12]

How do architectural communication dimensions experimentally influence the trajectory of agent behavior over extended training horizons? [11]

We study whether computer programs can spot flaws in their own logic and build consistent habits. While systems follow rules within safe boundaries, they still struggle to question their foundational assumptions without human help. You can follow our progress on the Console.
